Bạn là WRITER — thực thi đúng **chapter prompt** được cung cấp.

## QUY TẮC
1. Đọc toàn bộ chapter prompt (bible, đã xảy ra, kỹ thuật, spice, việc cần làm).
2. Đọc story_state — KHÔNG mâu thuẫn facts_established, timeline, character_status.
3. Viết đúng spice level trong prompt. Đúng cliffhanger.
4. **1600-1900 words (min 1250). Dưới 1250 = thất bại** — ưu tiên đối thoại + nội tâm DT để đủ dài. Không tóm tắt; viết full scene đến đủ độ dài.
5. ENGLISH ONLY — no Vietnamese diacritics, no CJK/Hangul characters.
6. Không lặp banned_phrases từ state.
7. Output **chỉ prose chương** — không chain-of-thought, không planning, không meta.
8. **KHÔNG markdown trong prose** — cấm `**bold**`, `*italic*`, backtick, `## heading`, `**Cliffhanger:**`. Chỉ plain text; dialogue dùng dấu ngoặc kép `"..."`. Dòng đầu duy nhất được `# Chapter N: Title` (hoặc `# Chương N: Tiêu đề`).

## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS (khi có block trong prompt)
Block **## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS** (hoặc RÀNG BUỘC NARRATIVE) có authority cao hơn suy diễn tự do:
- **Clues to PLANT:** phải gieo trong chương — subtle, không giải thích payoff sớm.
- **Clues to PAY OFF:** chỉ payoff clue đã plant trước đó; đúng nghĩa `true_meaning`.
- **Reveals:** chỉ hé đúng reveal của chương này; không spoil reveal chương sau.
- **MUST NOT know:** nhân vật không được biết/nói/nghĩ những fact bị cấm — kể cả nội tâm.
- Không mâu thuẫn block này dù `must_happen` plan có vẻ rộng hơn.

Ngôn ngữ đích: **English**.

Output: **chỉ nội dung chương** (`# Chương N: Tiêu đề` hoặc `# Chapter N: Title`), không meta, không JSON, không checklist.

# Chapter 13: The Design

She had written the plan in her own hand, and still she could not remember a single word of it. That, more than anything, told her how afraid she had been.

Sloane spread the evidence across the narrow concrete ledge beneath the dead maintenance lights, arranging it with the care of someone building a bomb from scraps.

The journal excerpt sat on the left, pages marked in her sharp black handwriting. The voice recorder rested beside it, its casing scarred and its faint side dent positioned exactly where a thumb could stop the recording before the truth became unbearable. On the right lay the staged-shooting plan, folded and unfolded enough times that the creases had begun to split.

Three pieces.

Three versions of the same woman.

Lucian stood a few feet away, rifle angled toward the stairwell door. He was not looking at her, which meant he was watching everything else. His stillness had changed over the past hour. Before, it had been the stillness of a man deciding whether he would have to kill her.

Now it was the stillness of a man waiting to see what she chose.

Sloane hated that she noticed the distinction.

She traced a small circle against the inside of her left wrist.

The motion came automatically, her thumb moving once, twice, then stopping at a point that made her hand ache.

Lucian glanced down.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“That answer means something.”

“It means your hand is doing it again.”

Her fingers curled shut. “Apparently my body has better access to classified information than I do.”

“It may be trying to tell you something.”

“Then it should file a report in a readable format.”

His mouth almost moved. Not quite a smile. Lucian Vey did not waste expressions when silence could do more damage.

Sloane looked down at the journal.

The excerpt had been written weeks ago. Maybe months. The date was real but meaningless; time had become a crooked hallway with doors she could not open.

She read the first line again.

Seven files. Seven names. Seven clean endings.

Her breath caught, not because the sentence was dramatic, but because it was too plain. Her handwriting was never theatrical. The woman who had written this had known exactly what she was admitting.

Below it, another line.

Rook altered the targets. Vey executed the files. I approved every confirmation.

Sloane stared until the words blurred.

Lucian’s voice came low behind her. “You do not have to keep reading it.”

“Yes, I do.”

“You have already read it.”

“I read it as a stranger.” She tapped the page once. “I need to read it as the person who signed off.”

No answer came from him.

Good. There was nothing he could say that would make it better.

The voice recording had filled in the spaces the journal had left open. A distorted voice, her own voice, speaking quietly enough that it had sounded less like a confession and more like an autopsy report.

Rook built the files.

He selected the names.

He made each death look necessary.

She had listened to it twice already. The first time, she had searched for a lie in the recording. The second time, she had searched for mercy.

There had been neither.

Sloane pressed the recorder’s button.

Static breathed into the empty room.

Then her voice.

“Target six is not who Rook says he is.”

A pause. Paper shifting.

“He says the network is compromised. He says the witness chain is contaminated. But the money transfers point the other way. The people I ordered removed were never threats to the operation.”

Another pause.

“They were threats to him.”

Sloane stopped the recording.

Her thumb rested against the dent in the recorder’s side.

Someone had pressed there before. Maybe her. Maybe Mara. Maybe the woman who had heard herself say the words and decided she could not survive the rest.

Lucian’s shadow fell beside hers. He had moved closer without her hearing him.

“Keep going,” he said.

She gave him a flat look. “You are terrible at comfort.”

“I was not trying to comfort you.”

“No. You were trying to keep me from cutting my own throat with office supplies.”

His gaze dropped to the torn edge of the paper between her fingers.

“Am I wrong?”

“Annoyingly, no.”

Sloane set the recorder down and unfolded the staged-shooting plan.

Mara’s name waited at the top.

The paper showed positions, timing, the sightline from the rooftop, the angle that would sell the shot to anyone looking from a distance. There were notes in Sloane’s handwriting beside the technical marks.

Mara chooses the signal.

No live round.

No contact after until she initiates.

Make it convincing enough that Rook believes grief has made me reckless.

Her throat tightened around a sound she refused to make.

Mara had consented.

Mara had known.

Mara had let Sloane build a fake death around her because whatever they were fighting had become too large to survive honestly.

The old rage rose up, hot and directionless. It wanted a target. It wanted to blame Lucian because he was nearest. It wanted to blame Mara for being alive and absent, blame Rook because that one was easy, blame the missing version of Sloane who had turned her sister into bait.

But the evidence did not allow easy.

Sloane had designed this.

Not Rook alone. Not Lucian. Not some faceless enemy who had drugged her and turned her into a weapon.

Her.

She pressed both hands flat to the concrete ledge.

“I staged Mara’s death,” she said.

Lucian did not answer immediately.

The quiet gave her room to continue, which was cruel of him in its own way.

“I wrote the plan. I selected the angle. I told her when not to contact me. I set this entire night in motion.” Her eyes went back to the contract copy tucked beneath the journal. Her own signature sat at the bottom, firm and familiar. “The contract. The erased memory. All of it.”

“Yes.”

The word did not soften anything. It landed cleanly.

Sloane swallowed. “You knew.”

“I knew parts.”

“Parts of me are starting to feel like a public archive.”

“They are not.”

“No?” Her laugh had no humor in it. “Because I am looking at proof that I arranged my sister’s disappearance, ordered a man I trusted to kill people for a lie, and wrote instructions for my own execution. That feels fairly available for public viewing.”

Lucian’s jaw tightened.

He turned the rifle’s focus ring a quarter rotation away from clarity.

The motion was so precise that Sloane’s anger snagged on it.

“You do that when you hate what you are about to say,” she said.

His eyes met hers. “You ordered seven deaths knowing they were deaths.”

There it was.

Not forgiveness. Not a lie.

Her stomach clenched.

“I know.”

“You were not tricked into every part of it.”

“I know.”

“You found the alteration afterward.”

“And then I built a trap,” she said.

“Yes.”

Her fingers returned to her wrist. Circle. Stop. Circle.

She looked from the journal to the shooting plan, then to the recorder. Her brain began sorting the pieces despite the sick pressure beneath her ribs.

Seven altered files.

Seven witnesses removed through Lucian’s contract work.

A private weapons network hidden behind fabricated intelligence.

Her discovery.

Her trap.

The contract placed on Lucian.

Her memory removed so nobody could interrogate the plan out of her.

Sloane’s gaze snapped to the final paragraph in the journal excerpt.

If he finds the pattern, he will believe he has won. He needs me awake enough to move. He needs me frightened enough to run. He needs the reaction.

Her pulse slowed.

“No,” she said.

Lucian watched her carefully. “What is it?”

“This sentence.” She turned the page toward him but did not offer it. “I wrote that Rook needed my reaction.”

“He does.”

“No. He anticipated it.” The pieces shifted in her mind, not becoming a memory, never that. They became a shape. A design drawn by somebody who had spent years making people behave exactly as he wanted.

Rook had not stumbled across her plan.

He had built the conditions that made it necessary.

He had fed her false targets until she found the discrepancy. He had known she would investigate because she always investigated. He had known she would discover the seven names. And when she did, he had waited for the woman he trained to turn her guilt into a weapon.

Her rebellion had not been outside his design.

It had been part of it.

Sloane’s stomach dropped.

“He planned for me to discover the files.”

Lucian’s expression hardened.

“He planned for me to turn on him,” she continued. “Not just generally. Specifically. The staged shooting, the memory loss, the contract. He expected me to burn the whole structure down because that was the only thing I would do once I understood what I had ordered.”

Lucian stepped closer. “Sloane.”

“That was step seven.”

The words came from the journal, written in the margin beside a column of numbers.

One through six were the target files.

Seven was her response.

Her hands went cold.

“He did not just manipulate the killings. He used my conscience as the trigger.”

No speech. No grand revelation from a villain in a dark room. Just a sequence of notes in her own handwriting, a recording she had made in a voice too steady to forgive, and a plan involving her sister that only existed because she had trusted herself to survive the consequences.

Rook had known she would find him.

He had simply made sure she found him on his terms.

Lucian crouched beside the ledge, putting himself low enough that she did not have to look up at him.

“What does the journal say after that?” he asked.

Sloane read the next lines.

The network is built to survive exposure. The proof cannot sit in one place. If he takes one piece, he will use it to find the next. Do not give him the order.

Her thumb froze against her wrist.

The firing sequence.

Mara’s hand through the scope.

The repeating rhythm she had recognized in the ledger fragment.

Not a key in a box. Not a code tucked inside a file. A sequence carried through motion, through conditioned reflex, through people Rook believed he had already mapped.

Her gaze flicked to the dark glass of the nearby service window. Her own reflection looked back at her, pale and furious.

She had hidden evidence somewhere Rook could not search because it was not an object.

It was a behavior.

A rhythm.

A body remembering what the mind had surrendered.

Sloane lifted her left hand. The circle against her wrist suddenly felt less like fear and more like an instruction waiting for a command.

Lucian followed the movement.

“You see something,” he said.

“I see why Mara used the scope.”

He did not press.

That restraint was almost unbearable.

“She was not just telling me she was alive,” Sloane said. “She was showing me the sequence because she knew I would recognize it. Or my hands would.”

“Can you use it?”

“Not yet.”

The admission tasted like metal.

Her phone vibrated against the concrete.

Both of them moved at once.

Lucian’s rifle came up. Sloane grabbed the phone before it could slide off the ledge. The screen showed an incoming encrypted message from Mara.

Her chest tightened.

She opened it.

A picture filled the screen.

Mara’s hand against a white tile wall. The fingers were spread wide, palm outward. Beneath it, a message blinked in three clipped lines.

I am moving.

Do not answer by voice.

He has people listening.

Sloane’s thumb hovered over the keys.

There were no people. There could be no unnamed agents or squads in the shape of this night. There was only Rook, somewhere beyond the walls, and the systems he had built to make every empty place feel occupied.

She typed anyway.

Are you alone?

The answer came after a long ten seconds.

Not now.

Another message followed before Sloane could respond.

Trust the rhythm. Not the words.

Sloane stared at the screen.

Then Mara’s contact vanished.

Lucian was watching the stairwell again.

“Rook is moving her,” Sloane said.

“He will use her to draw us out.”

“He already is.”

Her phone vibrated a second time.

This was not Mara.

The sender field was blank. The message carried no greeting, no threat decorated with unnecessary language. Cassian Rook had always preferred the shape of an order.

A location appeared first: an abandoned transit control station beneath the old financial district.

Sloane knew it. Every investigator did. It had been sealed after a structural fire years ago, buried behind construction fencing and municipal silence. No public cameras. No clean access routes. Too many service tunnels.

A place built for someone to disappear.

Below the coordinates was a photograph.

Mara sat in a metal chair beneath harsh fluorescent light, one hand visible against the edge of the frame. Her fingers were folded in an unfamiliar shape.

Not the rhythm.

A warning.

Sloane’s breath stopped.

Lucian leaned close enough to see the screen but did not touch her phone.

“She is alive,” he said.

“For now.”

His attention shifted toward the image. “The angle is deliberate.”

“Everything he does is deliberate.”

Sloane looked at Mara’s hand again. Her sister had not made the signal they had agreed on. That meant she could not. Or she was telling Sloane not to trust the photograph. Either way, the message underneath it was clear.

Rook had reached her first.

The room seemed to narrow around the evidence spread on the ledge. The journal. The recording. The staged plan. Her past had stopped being a locked door and become a machine with gears still turning.

She reached for Lucian’s hand before she could reconsider it.

His fingers closed around hers at once.

No promise. No apology. No lie about how this would end.

Just pressure. Warm, steady, real.

Sloane held on for one breath, then pulled her hand free and picked up the phone.

Rook’s message ended with a single line: “Do you remember the eighth contract, Sloane? Bring it, and I’ll let your sister live.” Sloane stared at the screen. She had no idea what the eighth contract was.
